title: Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks
abstract: Large Convolutional Network models have recently demonstrated impressive classification performance on the ImageNet benchmark. However there is no clear understanding of why they perform so well, or how they might be improved. In this paper we address both issues. We introduce a novel visualization technique that gives insight into the function of intermediate feature layers and the operation of the classifier. We also perform an ablation study to discover the performance contribution from different model layers. This enables us to find model architectures that outperform Krizhevsky \etal on the ImageNet classification benchmark. We show our ImageNet model generalizes well to other datasets: when the softmax classifier is retrained, it convincingly beats the current state-of-the-art results on Caltech-101 and Caltech-256 datasets.
research_question: Why do large convolutional network models perform so well on image classification, and how can they be improved?
core_contribution: Introduces a novel visualization technique using a deconvnet to understand intermediate feature layers in convolutional networks, which is used to diagnose and improve model architecture, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet and demonstrating strong feature generalization to other datasets.
conclusion: The deconvnet visualization technique provides insight into the function of convolutional networks, enabling architectural improvements and demonstrating the transferability of learned features to other datasets.
key_findings: Feature visualizations reveal hierarchical, increasingly invariant, and class-discriminative representations in higher layers.
Visualization diagnostics led to architectural changes (smaller filters, reduced stride) that improved ImageNet classification performance.
Occlusion experiments show the model's classification is sensitive to local object structure, not just global scene context.
Features from an ImageNet-trained convnet generalize well to other datasets (Caltech-101, Caltech-256) with only the softmax classifier retrained.
Ablation studies indicate the depth of the network is crucial for good performance, more so than the size of individual layers.
limitation: The model generalizes less well to PASCAL VOC 2012, possibly due to dataset bias, and its single-label classification loss is not suited for images containing multiple objects.
future_direction: Using a different loss function that permits multiple objects per image to improve performance on detection tasks.
